introduction: “We, verily, have made music as a ladder for your souls,” Bahá’u’lláh writes, and adds the warning that it not be made “wings to self and passion.” The readings that follow are mostly ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s: music as food for the spirit, as something children should be taught well and artists should perfect, as the proper sound of worship, and, in letter after letter in the manner of the Persian poets, as the figure for joy itself, with nightingale, harp, lute and wine. David is the readings’ own patron, and the psalms supply much of the company, with Miriam’s timbrel, Elisha’s minstrel and the morning stars. Plato, Aristotle and Confucius agree that music forms character. The poets hear what the readings hear in a reaper’s song or a piper’s tune. The cautions come from Augustine, uneasy at his own tears, from Tolstoy, who distrusted music’s power, from Amos, who wanted justice more than songs, from Tagore, and from Proverbs and Shakespeare on singing to a heavy heart.
questions: Music is “a ladder for your souls” and may become “wings to self and passion.” Orsino feeds his mood on it and Tolstoy’s narrator fears it. By what signs do you tell the two uses apart in your own listening?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá wants children taught “the best” music, and Plato and Aristotle hold that music forms character. What follows for how a family or community chooses its music, and where would Plato’s ban on innovation go too far?

The readings distinguish a garden bird’s passing song from the “spiritual nightingale,” while Keats, Shelley and Wordsworth find something lasting in a bird or a reaper. Is the difference in the music, the musician, or the hearer?
Amos asks for justice before songs and charges those who chant to the viol with forgetting the afflicted. How can a community that loves music and joy keep his question in view?
A grieving friend is told to sing and not lament; Proverbs and Shakespeare’s Malcolm say grief must have its words. When is each counsel the kind one?
“When the earthly music is joined with the heavenly music … the spirits will soar.” What, in practice, joins them: the words, the intention of the performer, the occasion, or the skill?

outside.why: “They who recite the verses of the All-Merciful in the most melodious of tones.” The Qur’án gives the same instruction for its own recitation: chant the Qur’án in measure.

Music is “a ladder for your souls”; “make it not … as wings to self and passion.” Shakespeare’s Orsino wants exactly what is warned against, music to feed his mood until appetite sickens. What turns the same melody into one or the other?
Mere “vibrations in the air,” and yet “see how they move the heart.” Congreve’s line of 1697 is the proverb for it: music has charms to soothe a savage breast, to soften rocks, or bend a knotted oak.
The musician’s art “moveth the hearts of all who grieve.” The song in Henry VIII says the same of Orpheus and his lute: in sweet music is such art, killing care and grief of heart.

“Among certain nations of the East, music was considered reprehensible.” Augustine shows why a serious believer could hesitate: he wept at the hymns, and feared the times when the singing moved him more than the thing sung.
Music as “spiritual food for soul and heart.” When the evil spirit was upon Saul, David took an harp and played, so Saul was refreshed, and was well.

Music has “wonderful sway and effect in the hearts of children.” Aristotle argued in the Politics that music has a power of forming the character and should therefore be introduced into the education of the young.
Children’s hearts are pure, “and melodies have great influence in them.” Plato gives the reason he puts music first in schooling: rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul.
“One must endeavour to attain the degree of artistic perfection.” The psalmist asks for craft as well as praise: sing unto him a new song; play skilfully.

A melody “bringeth the very spirit of life” to one heart and “staineth with lust” another. Tolstoy’s narrator in The Kreutzer Sonata goes further and distrusts the power itself: music makes me forget my real situation; it transports me into a state which is not my own. Is that power innocent in itself?
Hymns of praise in the house of worship “to enrapture the Concourse on High.” The last psalm lists the instruments: trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organs, cymbals.

Verses chanted “at large gatherings and congregations in a most wondrous melody.” Milton on what the organ and the full-voiced choir did to him: dissolve me into ecstasies, and bring all heaven before mine eyes.
Perfect the art and “serve at the threshold.” The psalmist joins the two for a lifetime: while I live will I praise the Lord; I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.

When art is studied “with the intention of obeying the command,” the study itself goes well. George Herbert’s prayer: teach me in all things thee to see, and what I do in anything, to do it as for thee.
Others discover “this fragrance of spirituality in the action itself.” Confucius asks what art is without the person: if a man be without the virtues proper to humanity, what has he to do with music?

Children are to be taught “the best, classical music, such masterpieces that refine the souls.” Plato was so sure of music’s effect on character that he would allow a city no new kind of song at all. How far should care about what children hear go?

A life that has learned music’s “artistic value and moral significance” is “redolent with brightness.” Shakespeare states the converse: the man that hath no music in himself is fit for treasons, stratagems and spoils.

Teach “the harmonies that exalt the spirit and ennoble one’s thoughts.” Confucius’s order of formation: the mind is aroused by the Odes, established by the rules of propriety, and from music the finish is received.
A beautiful voice is to be cultivated so that the prayers may be chanted “with effect.” Paul: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
The voice must be trained. Paul on why precision matters: if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?
A new “Song of the Covenant” is sung in great assemblages. The psalm’s command: O sing unto the Lord a new song; sing unto the Lord, all the earth.
A hymn written in America is sent to Persia to be translated and sung. Zephaniah foresees peoples given a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord with one consent.

“All poems shall be forgotten in the course of time save those that are extraordinary.” Shakespeare makes the same promise to his own sonnet: not marble, nor the gilded monuments of princes, shall outlive this powerful rhyme.

Poems of these days will be sung “after a thousand years.” Keats heard such permanence in a nightingale, whose song was heard in ancient days by emperor and clown. The bird’s song lasts because it is no one’s. What makes a hymn last?
“Music is an ancient art.” Genesis sets it near the beginning of all arts: Jubal was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
A lad on a donkey plays his flute by the Euphrates, and the hearer stops him to listen. Wordsworth heard a girl singing at her reaping: the music in my heart I bore, long after it was heard no more.
The piper asked to play again. Blake’s piper is stopped by a child on a cloud: piper, pipe that song again; so I piped: he wept to hear.
When the vina began, the piano overhead fell silent. Elijah on the mountain hears wind, earthquake and fire, and after them a still small voice.
One music gives way before another. Habakkuk: the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.
“Both words and music make the song.” Colossians keeps the two together: let the word dwell in you richly, in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts.

The ship’s musicians played, “the listeners clapped their hands and all was ended.” Ezekiel was told he had become that to his hearers: a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice; they hear thy words, but they do them not.
The gladness of singing “is transitory and will be forgotten within a short time.” The Preacher counted his men singers and women singers among the delights that proved vanity.
Tunes blended with “the melodies of the Kingdom” give solace. Isaiah promises a people a song as in the night when a holy solemnity is kept, and gladness of heart.

“The effect of a garden bird’s song lasts but a moment.” Shelley heard in a skylark a spirit pouring its full heart from heaven or near it. Is the line between the bird in the garden and the “spiritual nightingale” as firm as the reading draws it?

High notes, instruments and dancers “bring no delight”; devotion does. Paul: though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.

It is “the melody of devotion and entreaty that bestows abundant joy.” Amos names something else that God wants more than melody: take away from me the noise of thy songs; let judgment run down as waters.
An ear that “seeks no thrill from any tune except this divine song.” The psalmist in exile: in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life.

Most people “are not endowed with ears to listen” to the heavenly music. Lorenzo to Jessica under the stars: such harmony is in immortal souls, but whilst this muddy vesture of decay doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it.
Ears “accustomed to such cheap rag time.” Isaiah’s complaint is of the same kind: the harp and the viol, the tabret and pipe are in their feasts, but they regard not the work of the Lord.

When the Bird of Paradise sings, “the buzzings of the bees are not heeded.” The Preacher ranks what the ear takes in: it is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools.
“Divine melody hath another effect, and heavenly song another.” John hears harpers harping before the throne, and a new song that no man could learn but the redeemed.
“If there are those who have good voices, sing.” The psalm asks no more than that: make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all the earth; make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise.
Persian chanting is welcomed in New York. The exiles in Babylon hung up their harps: how shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land? What has to be true for a people’s sacred music to travel?
A meeting for worship: prayer chanted, readings “with melodious voices … by all together.” The last supper ends the same way: when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives.

The reading arranges chanting and communion in a room. Tagore: leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads; thy God is where the tiller is tilling the hard ground. What keeps a meeting for worship from being the shut temple he describes?
“No musician played melodies and songs,” yet the gathering was radiant. Keats on the pipes painted on an urn: heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter.
Song raised “to bring the dwellers of the Kingdom into rapture.” Luke has it flow the other way on one night: a multitude of the heavenly host praising God.
When they gather “they sing sweet melodies and offer praise.” Ephesians: speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.
To sing praises and “become the cause of joy and gladness to all.” James’s plain rule: is any merry? let him sing psalms.

Educated women “raise such a call” of praise that heaven is attracted. Miriam the prophetess took a timbrel in her hand, and all the women went out after her; and Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the Lord.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s “supreme joy” is the voices of women raised in praise. A sentence in First Corinthians, long used to settle the matter, says: let your women keep silence in the churches. How have communities lived with both Miriam and this verse?
A talent for music is to be used “in prayer and supplication.” The psalmist’s resolve: I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live.
A singer’s voice “reached the ears” of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and gave joy. Zephaniah imagines God himself as the one who sings: he will joy over thee with singing.
A letter in which every word is an instrument: “a perfect symphony.” At the dedication of Solomon’s temple the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound.
The symphony depends on every part. Shakespeare’s Ulysses on what follows when one string goes: untune that string, and hark, what discord follows.
Chanted “in the gathering of the friends,” and hearts became joyful. The psalm that was itself a pilgrims’ song: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Poems intoned “on the way.” Isaiah’s travellers: the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads.
A household “all engaged in melody and joy,” each with a song. Whitman heard a nation that way: each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else.
“With melody, song, chanting, ecstasy, attraction and rapture” at the threshold. David danced before the Lord with all his might, with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet.
“Each one … must take up the lute and reed.” The psalmist to his instruments: awake, psaltery and harp; I myself will awake early.
“Singing songs and melodies out of intense joy and delight is desirable.” The hundredth psalm: serve the Lord with gladness; come before his presence with singing.
“Show forth ecstasy and joy!” Schiller’s ode, which Beethoven set for chorus, calls all people brethren under joy’s wing.
“Why are you silent and quiet? Raise a cry.” Told to quiet his disciples’ praise, Jesus answers: if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
The lute plays, and the gathering is “lifeless.” Jesus quotes the children’s complaint in the marketplace: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced.

Tones that stir “the spirit of possibility” and gladden “the hearts of the people of all worlds.” A psalm lets creation join: let the heavens rejoice, let the field be joyful, then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice.
A song at which “the Angel of the highest heaven will be moved.” Jesus speaks of joy in the presence of the angels of God.

The readings borrow the Persian poets’ tavern: wine, cup, intoxication, harp and lute. Ephesians sets the two side by side: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns.
“It is time for song and melody.” The Song of Solomon: the winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth, the time of the singing of birds is come.
Pass beyond “the desolate wilds of remoteness” and hold a festival to harp and lute. When the prodigal comes home, his brother in the field hears music and dancing.

The nightingale is the sweet singer the East prefers. Sa‘dí tells that bird of the morning to learn love from the moth, which burned, gave its life, and found no voice. Is there a devotion beyond song?
Odes “in praise of the All-Knowing God.” The psalm of thanksgiving: enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise.

Wine from the tavern, given to the friends. Khayyám’s quatrain, in FitzGerald’s English, has the same furniture and a different heaven: a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and thou beside me singing in the wilderness.

“Tune the harp of love” so that its echo reaches East and West. Tagore to his God: this little flute of a reed thou hast carried over hills and dales, and hast breathed through it melodies eternally new.
A song for both East and West. The psalm’s compass for praise: from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same.
“Chant songs of joy, strike up a melody.” Isaiah: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
“We are drunk with the cup of ‘Am I not?’” The song quotes the Qur’án’s scene of the first covenant: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily.
“Make thou no lamentation … but instead chant melodies.” Paul and Silas, beaten and in the stocks: at midnight they prayed, and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them.

A grieving friend is told to sing. Proverbs warns the comforter: as he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart. When does a call to joy help, and when does it hurt?
“Not for sighs and groans and constant wailing.” Malcolm to a man who has just lost everything: give sorrow words; the grief that does not speak whispers the o’er-fraught heart and bids it break.
“This is the time for the wisdom of Solomon and the melody of David.” The Preacher on times: to every thing there is a season.
“Where have the sounds of lute and organ gone?” Lamentations asks it of a fallen city: the young men have ceased from their musick; our dance is turned into mourning.
The secrets of string and reed. Rúmí opens his great poem with a reed flute whose whole music is complaint: listen to the reed, how it tells of separations.
“Silence and stillness appear forsaken and unfortunate.” A psalm makes stillness the way of knowing: be still, and know that I am God. What does each season of the soul need?
A melody by which “the mysteries [will] be unfolded.” Elisha, asked for a word, calls for a minstrel; and when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him.
“With harp and drum and reed and strings.” The psalter’s last line: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord.
“When the earthly music is joined with the heavenly music.” Job is told of the first such concert, when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.
“Begin playing the psalms of the House of David.” One of them says where its song came from: he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God.
Laughing and joyous, with songs “that would bring the listener to dance.” The psalmist: thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing; thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness.

Wine-flask, song and rapture are the reading’s images of joy. Amos uses the same scene for a charge: they chant to the sound of the viol and drink wine in bowls, but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. What keeps rapture from forgetting the afflicted?
Birds on the branches “teach lessons … with meaningful melodies.” The Qur’án: the birds in their flight, each knoweth its worship and its praise.
At times the tune of lovers, at times “the sighs and lamentations of the yearning ones.” Shelley: our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought.
“Thou must come with the old song.” Tennyson’s bells are told the opposite: ring out the old, ring in the new. Which songs does a renewed faith keep?
A bird told that its time to sing has come. Emily Dickinson’s bird needs no telling: hope is the thing with feathers, that sings the tune without the words, and never stops at all.
A melody at which “the birds of the meadow may come.” The Qur’án says of David: O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise.
A player “in harmony and concert with the birds of the world.” The Qur’án: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise.
Play “that you may discover the hidden mysteries.” The psalmist expects to arrive by the same road: then will I go unto God my exceeding joy; yea, upon the harp will I praise thee.
Other birds “cry out and lament,” but the nightingale of faithfulness sings. Blake asks about the bird that cannot: how can the bird that is born for joy sit in a cage and sing?
“Every bird that raises its voice … is indeed a nightingale.” The psalm is as generous: it is good to sing praises; praise is comely.

A melody by which listeners “pass beyond name and fame” and are bewildered by “the unlimited Reality.” Coleridge, listening to a wind-harp: the one Life within us and abroad, a light in sound, rhythm in all thought.
Song on the day of meeting that will “cause a tumult in that city.” What was said of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica: these that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.

keats-heard-melodies.text: Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on; / Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear'd, / Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone
keats-heard-melodies.author: John Keats

keats-immortal-bird.text: Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird! / No hungry generations tread thee down; / The voice I hear this passing night was heard / In ancient days by emperor and clown
keats-immortal-bird.author: John Keats

shelley-sweetest-songs.text: We look before and after, / And pine for what is not: / Our sincerest laughter / With some pain is fraught; / Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought
shelley-sweetest-songs.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

shelley-unpremeditated-art.text: Hail to thee, blithe spirit! / Bird thou never wert, / That from heaven, or near it, / Pourest thy full heart / In profuse strains of unpremeditated art
shelley-unpremeditated-art.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

wordsworth-music-in-my-heart.text: I listened till I had my fill: / And, as I mounted up the hill, / The music in my heart I bore, / Long after it was heard no more
wordsworth-music-in-my-heart.author: William Wordsworth

whitman-america-singing.text: I hear America singing, the varied carols I hear, / Those of mechanics, each one singing his as it should be blithe and strong … Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else
whitman-america-singing.author: Walt Whitman

tolstoy-music-transports-me.text: Music makes me forget my real situation. It transports me into a state which is not my own. Under the influence of music I really seem to feel what I do not feel, to understand what I do not understand, to have powers which I cannot have
tolstoy-music-transports-me.author: Leo Tolstoy

plato-musical-innovation.text: any musical innovation is full of danger to the whole State, and ought to be prohibited
plato-musical-innovation.author: Plato

aristotle-music-forming-the-character.text: music has a power of forming the character, and should therefore be introduced into the education of the young. The study is suited to the stage of youth, for young persons will not, if they can help, endure anything which is not sweetened by pleasure, and music has a natural sweetness
aristotle-music-forming-the-character.author: Aristotle

congreve-music-has-charms.text: Musick has Charms to sooth a savage Breast, / To soften Rocks, or bend a knotted Oak
congreve-music-has-charms.author: William Congreve

shakespeare-food-of-love.text: If music be the food of love, play on; / Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken, and so die
shakespeare-food-of-love.author: William Shakespeare

shakespeare-in-sweet-music-is-such-art.text: Orpheus with his lute made trees, / And the mountain tops that freeze, / Bow themselves when he did sing … In sweet music is such art, / Killing care and grief of heart / Fall asleep, or hearing, die
shakespeare-in-sweet-music-is-such-art.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-in-sweet-music-is-such-art.caveat: The play was written with John Fletcher, to whom this song is often assigned.

psalm-play-skilfully.text: Praise the Lord with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings. Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise

psalm-new-song-in-my-mouth.text: And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the Lord

psalm-in-the-night-his-song.text: Yet the Lord will command his lovingkindness in the day time, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life

exodus-miriam-took-a-timbrel.text: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances. And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea

samuel-david-danced.text: And David danced before the Lord with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet

chronicles-as-one-to-make-one-sound.text: It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the Lord; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the Lord, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud

ecclesiastes-men-singers-and-women-singe.text: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts

ecclesiastes-song-of-fools.text: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools

amos-chant-to-the-sound-of-the-viol.text: That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David; That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph

isaiah-harp-and-viol-in-their-feasts.text: Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them! And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the Lord, neither consider the operation of his hands

luke-musick-and-dancing.text: Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing. And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant. And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound. And he was angry, and would not go in

corinthians-uncertain-sound.text: And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle

corinthians-sing-with-the-understanding.text: What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also

revelation-harpers-harping.text: And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps: And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred and forty and four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth

psalm-joyful-noise-with-harp-and-trumpet.text: Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise. Sing unto the Lord with the harp; with the harp, and the voice of a psalm. With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the Lord, the King

psalm-sing-as-long-as-i-live.text: I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being

matthew-sung-an-hymn.text: And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives

lamentations-dance-turned-into-mourning.text: The elders have ceased from the gate, the young men from their musick. The joy of our heart is ceased; our dance is turned into mourning

isaiah-song-as-in-the-night.text: Ye shall have a song, as in the night when a holy solemnity is kept; and gladness of heart, as when one goeth with a pipe to come into the mountain of the Lord, to the mighty One of Israel

quran-hills-and-birds-echo.text: And assuredly We gave David grace from Us, (saying): O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise! And We made the iron supple unto him,

blake-piping-down-the-valleys.text: Piping down the valleys wild / Piping songs of pleasant glee / On a cloud I saw a child. / And he laughing said to me / Pipe a song about a Lamb / So I piped with merry chear. / Piper pipe that song again / So I piped, he wept to hear
blake-piping-down-the-valleys.author: William Blake
